The etalon has a mirror radius of 31 cm, thickness of 30 cm, and beam radius of 12 cm.
The front surface of the etalon has 3 doublets of coating layers, and the back surface has 17 doublets.
The mechanical loss angle (φ) for the silica layers is 4×10^-5 and for the tantala layers is 2×10^-4.
The amplitude reflectivity of the front coating is r1 = 0.834 and of the back coating is r2 = 1 - 1.36×10^-5.
The force coefficient for the front surface is ǫ1 = 0.869 and for the back surface is ǫ2 = 0.131.
The Young's modulus for silica is 7.2×10^10 Pa and for tantala is 1.4×10^11 Pa.
The Poisson's ratio for silica is 0.17 and for tantala is 0.23.
The refractive index for silica is 1.45 and for tantala is 2.035.
The total thermal noise level of the etalon can be a factor of ~1.7 times better than a single mirror with the same reflectivity.
Increasing the etalon thickness further reduces the thermal noise level, though thermorефractive noise will increase.
The thermorефractive noise is found to be a few orders of magnitude smaller than the coating thermal noise with the given parameters.
The analytical model was verified by cross-checking with finite element analysis (FEA) simulations, which showed agreement within 5%.
In the thin mirror limit where the mechanical transfer from one surface to the other is almost direct (η ≈ 1), the analytical results can be intuitively verified.
The main challenge of the etalon design is the increased complexity compared to a single mirror, but the paper shows it can provide significant noise reduction.
The etalon design separates the thermal fluctuations between the front and back surfaces, reducing the overall noise level.
